archetype.name: Lost Season (broken offense)
archetype.definition: A team two years removed from back-to-back 11-win seasons whose offense has collapsed to the bottom of the league, leaving a middling defense with no margin and a winless record that is worse than even its poor play.

report.headline: An offense that can't run, protect or hold the ball sank an 11-win roster.
report.take:
The Chargers are 0-8, and it isn't a fluke built on bad bounces alone. They rank last in net EPA, last in offensive EPA and last in offensive success rate. This is the same program that won 11 games in each of the last two seasons behind a top-six defense, so this is a collapse, not a rebuild that went as planned. The defense has slipped from elite to average, 15th in EPA allowed. The offense has gone from below average to the worst in football.

The offense's problem is its identity. Harbaugh's Chargers have the league's most run-heavy approach relative to the situation, a pass rate over expected of -11.4, and the league's worst rushing EPA at -0.267 a carry. They keep leaning on the thing that works least. When Justin Herbert does drop back, he is sacked on 10.5% of dropbacks, 31st in the league, even though the pressure rate allowed is only 21st. That gap says the pressure turns into sacks far too often, which points to the quarterback, receivers and play design as much as the line. Add a league-worst 4.9 line penalties a game and 19 turnovers, and drives die before they start.

The defense is better than the 27.4 points a game it allows. The scoreboard is skewed by an offense handing over the ball and short fields. The unit is 7th on third down, 2nd in rushing touchdowns allowed and 9th in takeaways. The record is also harsher than the play: the point differential implies 3.3 wins, and the -3.25 wins over expected is the worst in the league. With no one-score wins, some of the 0-8 is bad luck in close games.

The direction is still wrong. The early losses were tight, and the last three were not, ending with a 22-44 loss to Houston in which Herbert was sacked eight times and the defense gave up 391 passing yards. The schedule ahead has some soft defenses, so a few wins are there. But nothing in the profile suggests a fix to the core problem, an offense that can neither run efficiently nor protect its passer.

strengths.title: Defense wins the situational downs
strengths.body: The defense gets off the field on third down and stiffens near the goal line. It ranks 7th in third-down rate allowed and 2nd in rushing touchdowns allowed, and it has forced 12 takeaways, 9th in the league. That is a well-coached unit holding up despite its offense constantly putting it back on the field. Takeaways are streaky, including a five-takeaway game at Buffalo, but the third-down and red-zone work has been steady enough to trust.

strengths.title: Tight underneath coverage, WR1s contained
strengths.body: Short passing against the Chargers is a dead end, with -0.033 EPA allowed on short throws, 11th in the league. Opposing top receivers score 3.4 PPR points a game below their usual output, 6th-best. They also tackle well, with a 7.8% missed-tackle rate that ranks 9th. That holds as long as the secondary stays healthy, and the cornerback injury list is starting to thin it.

concerns.title: Run-first plan, league-worst run game
concerns.body: No team leans on the run more relative to situation, and no team gets less from it. The line's 2.28 yards before contact and 23.8% stuff rate mean the backs are hit early. Committing to the run anyway turns early downs into long third downs for a passing game that already struggles. This is a coaching choice as much as a personnel problem, and the season shows no sign of it changing.

concerns.title: Sacks, flags and giveaways kill drives
concerns.body: Herbert has been sacked 31 times, with eight in the Houston game alone. The line commits the most penalties in the league, and the offense has 19 turnovers for a -7 turnover margin. Those giveaways are the main reason a middle-of-the-pack defense allows 28th-ranked scoring. The sack rate running far ahead of the pressure rate makes this partly a quarterback-and-design issue, not just the blockers. With guard Kayode Awosika out, the protection is unlikely to get better soon.

concerns.title: No pass rush, leaky deep coverage
concerns.body: The rush gets home on only 18.8% of dropbacks, 24th, with 13 sacks, 30th. Without pressure, the deep secondary gets exposed, allowing 1.058 EPA on deep throws, 29th in the league. Houston's 391 passing yards showed what happens when a quarterback has time. This is a real drop from the 2025 defense, which ranked 6th in EPA allowed.

trend.note: The first five losses were all within two scores, and several came down to one possession. Since the bye the margins have widened, ending with a 44-point outing by Houston and an eight-sack day for Herbert.

nextGame.headline: Baltimore's quarterback crisis gives the winless Chargers a real opening.
nextGame.body:
The Chargers go to Baltimore as 5.5-point underdogs with a 38.5 total, which points to a low-scoring grind. Baltimore is an average team at 4-5, 20th in net EPA. It is vulnerable through the air, with a defense that ranks 31st in EPA allowed to opposing WR1s and 26th on deep balls. Its offense runs well, gaining 4.4 yards a carry (7th), but its line allows pressure at the 29th-ranked rate. Baltimore also goes for it on fourth down more than anyone, ranked 1st, and has the worse special teams of the two, at -2.19 EPA a game.

Availability is the story. Baltimore started Joe Fagnano in Week 9, with Lamar Jackson on IR after thumb surgery and Tyler Huntley on IR. Its secondary is also thin: Nate Wiggins and Jaylinn Hawkins are out and Kyle Hamilton is questionable with a hip injury. On the Chargers' side, Herbert is questionable with a finger injury that was not a fracture. Guard Kayode Awosika is out, Ladd McConkey is day to day with back spasms, and two backup corners are banged up.

waysToWin.title: Defense feasts on a backup quarterback
waysToWin.body: With both of Baltimore's top quarterbacks on IR, the Chargers' strong third-down defense and takeaway habit face their softest matchup of the year. Baltimore's line allows pressure at the 29th-ranked rate, so even a weak pass rush can get home. Short fields from takeaways are the most likely way this offense scores.

waysToWin.title: Attack a depleted Baltimore secondary
waysToWin.body: Baltimore is already among the worst in the league against WR1s and deep throws, and now it is missing Wiggins and Hawkins. This is the week for the Chargers to drop the run-first plan and let Herbert target Tre Harris and Quentin Johnston downfield. Whether Harbaugh actually opens it up is the question.

waysToWin.title: Win field position on special teams
waysToWin.body: In a game the Book expects to stay under 40 points, Baltimore's 27th-ranked special teams can hand over hidden yards. Its red-zone defense ranks 21st, so drives that start near midfield can end in touchdowns instead of field goals.

waysToLose.title: Giveaways and sacks hand over the game
waysToLose.body: This offense has beaten itself all year, and a backup Baltimore quarterback doesn't fix that. Another multi-turnover, four-sack day with a backup guard in the lineup gives Baltimore short fields it can't create on its own. A hurt finger for Herbert only adds to the ball-security risk.

waysToLose.title: Running into a wall again
waysToLose.body: Baltimore allows the 4th-fewest explosive runs, so the Chargers' run-heavy plan likely produces three-yard carries and long third downs. If Harbaugh sticks with it anyway, the league's worst rushing offense wastes the matchup against Baltimore's weak pass defense.

waysToLose.title: Baltimore grinds it on the ground
waysToLose.body: Baltimore can protect a backup quarterback by running the ball, and it ranks 7th in yards per carry against a Chargers run defense that is 21st in EPA. Add Baltimore's habit of going for it on fourth down, and long drives could keep the Chargers' offense off the field.

nextGame.watch: Whether Herbert plays, and whether the Chargers throw early against a Baltimore secondary missing Wiggins and Hawkins or default to the run.

restOfSeason.body:
Some correction is coming. A team with this point differential would normally have about three wins, and no team stays winless in one-score games forever. The schedule also offers chances: the Jets, Raiders and Dolphins all bring bottom-eight defenses, and Baltimore is down to its third quarterback. The defense's third-down and red-zone work should keep games closer than the recent blowouts.

What won't fix itself is the offense. The sack problem, the line penalties and a run-first plan with the league's worst run game are structural, and Herbert's finger and a thinning line add risk. San Francisco, Kansas City and Denver close out the year. Expect a few wins against the weak teams, an offense that stays in the bottom tier, and a draft position that comes into focus.
swingFactors: Herbert's finger and the state of the line
Whether Harbaugh lets the offense pass more
Close-game luck against the weak teams left on the schedule

confidence.note: Eight games of consistent offensive failure, but Herbert's health and Baltimore's quarterback situation are unknowns.
